handoff.reason: This hesperidin/metabolic-syndrome RCT is a RETRACTED PUBLICATION per the index metadata; kept here with retracted=True flagged but should not be used as standalone evidence.

identity_notes: Citrus bioflavonoids' retrieval set is dominated by a huge false-match cluster of unrelated medicinal plants (Cuscuta chinensis, Salvia officinalis, Sambucus nigra, Pistacia atlantica, Lycii Fructus, Apocynum venetum, Azolla pinnata, Indigofera argentea, Xanthoceras sorbifolium, Mentha spicata, hawthorn, Parthenocissus, buckwheat, oat, amaranth) and agricultural/crop-science studies on tomato, rice, wheat, cabbage, and microtomato -- all rejected off_topic, likely retrieved via generic 'flavonoid'/'rutin' keyword overlap rather than citrus specificity. A second large cluster is animal and in vitro mechanistic studies of hesperidin and rutin (rats, mice, cats, cell lines such as SH-SY5Y and HepG2) investigating toxicology/hepatoprotection/nephroprotection pathways -- rejected animal_or_invitro throughout, including several reviews that explicitly self-describe as covering 'in vitro and in vivo' or 'preclinical' evidence only. Among genuine human oral evidence, two coherent clinical clusters dominate: (1) hesperidin/diosmin-based VENOACTIVE DRUGS (Daflon/MPFF, diosmin-hesperidin combinations, hydroxyethylrutosides) for chronic venous insufficiency, hemorrhoidal disease, and varicose veins -- a long-established, well-studied drug class where hesperidin is typically the minor component alongside dominant diosmin, flagged related_form_differs; and (2) isolated hesperidin or rutin supplementation trials for type 2 diabetes, NAFLD, blood pressure/lipids, and cardiometabolic markers, where results are decidedly mixed across individual RCTs and meta-analyses (e.g., 30632207 and 31489695 found no effect on lipids/BP or glucose control respectively, while 28805022/29468764 and several diabetes RCTs found positive effects). A recurring pattern is hesperidin delivered in modified/glycosylated forms (alpha-glucosyl hesperidin, monoglucosyl hesperidin, 2S-hesperidin, hesperidin methyl chalcone, glucosyl hesperidin) developed specifically to overcome hesperidin's native low bioavailability -- these are flagged related_form_differs since they are chemically distinct from native hesperidin as typically declared on a supplement label. One retracted publication (31844967) was kept with retracted=True flagged and routed to handoff rather than silently discarded.
